subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Emergencies and Toxicology: BLS, Shock, Poisoning, and Envenomation

steps.tx: Cardiopulmonary arrest in children overwhelmingly results from progressive hypoxia and respiratory failure rather than sudden primary cardiac dysrhythmias. Under international guidelines for **paediatric basic life support**, resuscitation follows the C-A-B sequence (Compressions-Airway-Breathing). Chest compressions are delivered at a rate of one hundred to one hundred and twenty per minute, depressing the infant chest by four centimetres and child chest by five centimetres.
steps.say: Pediatric cardiopulmonary arrest is usually secondary to respiratory failure. Compress the chest at one hundred to one hundred and twenty per minute to one-third chest depth.

rows: 4 cm (1.5 inches) or 1/3 AP chest diameter
5 cm (2 inches) or 1/3 AP chest diameter
One or two hands on lower half of sternum
Ensure full chest recoil between compressions

steps.tx: Inadequate tissue perfusion failing to deliver oxygen and nutrients to vital organs defines acute shock. Early identification of **compensated versus decompensated pediatric shock** relies on blood pressure: in compensated shock, systemic vascular resistance rises to maintain normal blood pressure despite tachycardia and delayed capillary refill (>2 seconds), whereas hypotension signifies decompensated shock demanding urgent twenty millilitres per kilogram boluses of isotonic crystalloid.
steps.say: Compensated shock maintains blood pressure through tachycardia and vasoconstriction. Hypotension indicates decompensated shock, requiring rapid isotonic fluid boluses.

left.title: Compensated Shock Features
points: Blood pressure strictly within normal limits
Resting tachycardia out of proportion to fever
Cool, pale, mottled extremities with weak peripheral pulses

right.title: Decompensated Shock Hallmarks
points: Profound lethargy, stupor, or altered sensorium
Absent peripheral pulses and faint central pulses

steps.tx: Rapid initial clinical triage categorizes ill children according to urgency of intervention before complete diagnostic workup. Under WHO Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment (ETAT), children are triaged for **emergency signs and IMNCI danger signs**, identifying priority cases exhibiting obstructed breathing, severe respiratory distress, central cyanosis, signs of severe shock, coma or convulsions, and severe dehydration with lethargy.
steps.say: WHO ETAT triage screens for emergency signs including airway obstruction, central cyanosis, shock, and convulsions. Children with emergency signs receive immediate life-saving care.

rows: Obstructed breathing, central cyanosis, shock, coma
Foreign body, severe croup, septicaemia, DKA
Tiny infant (<2 mos), high fever, severe pain, respiratory distress
Rapid assessment, move to front of queue
Mild symptoms, chronic illness, healthy checkup
Unable to drink/breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargy

steps.tx: Accidental ingestion of volatile hydrocarbons in toddlers carries high risks of chemical pulmonary toxicity. In **accidental kerosene ingestion in toddlers**, the low viscosity and high volatility of liquid paraffin allow it to spread across the pharynx and penetrate the bronchial tree. Gastric lavage and emetics are strictly contraindicated, as inducing emesis dramatically increases aspiration risks, leading to necrotizing chemical pneumonitis.
steps.say: Never induce vomiting or perform gastric lavage in kerosene ingestion, as aspiration causes chemical pneumonitis. Observe for coughing and respiratory distress.

left.title: Pathophysiological Mechanisms
points: Low viscosity and low surface tension promote airway spread
Aspiration into alveoli dissolves pulmonary surfactant

right.title: Contraindicated Clinical Actions
points: Activated charcoal has zero efficacy for hydrocarbons
Observe for 6 hours; obtain chest X-ray if symptomatic

steps.tx: Irreversible organophosphate inhibition of acetylcholinesterase enzymes produces massive cholinergic accumulation across muscarinic and nicotinic synapses. Manifesting with the DUMBELS or SLUDGE syndrome, **pediatric organophosphate poisoning** causes pinpoint constricted pupils, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, diaphoresis, vomiting, diarrhea, and bradycardia. Immediate treatment requires intravenous atropine titrated to clear pulmonary secretions, followed by pralidoxime.
steps.say: Organophosphate poisoning causes pinpoint pupils, severe salivation, and wet lung secretions. Titrate intravenous atropine until lung secretions dry completely.

vis.alt: Diagram displaying synaptic accumulation of acetylcholine and dual antidotal mechanisms of atropine and pralidoxime.
vis.caption: Synaptic mechanism of organophosphate toxicity and pharmacological reversal using atropine and pralidoxime. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Specific pharmacological antidotes reverse life-threatening toxicities when administered rapidly following acute pediatric ingestions. In acute paracetamol overdose, **N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol poisoning** replenishes depleted hepatocellular glutathione pools, neutralizing the hepatotoxic metabolite NAPQI. In acute iron poisoning with serum iron exceeding five hundred micrograms per decilitre, intravenous deferoxamine chelation binds free circulating iron, imparting a vin-rose color to urine.
steps.say: Administer N-acetylcysteine within eight hours for paracetamol poisoning to replenish glutathione. Intravenous deferoxamine chelates toxic iron, turning urine a vin-rose color.

vis.alt: Educational visual displaying antidotes including N-acetylcysteine, deferoxamine, atropine, and naloxone for pediatric poisonings.
vis.caption: Specific pediatric antidotes and their clinical indications in acute childhood poisonings. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Cardiovascular collapse following Indian red scorpion envenomation arises from massive autonomic catecholamine storm. In **scorpion envenomation and prazosin therapy**, venom blocks voltage-gated potassium channels, releasing floods of epinephrine and norepinephrine. This induces intense alpha-1 receptor vasoconstriction, massive hypertension, acute left ventricular failure, and flash pulmonary edema. Oral prazosin (thirty micrograms per kilogram stat) acts as an essential physiological antidote.
steps.say: Indian red scorpion stings trigger an autonomic storm causing hypertension and pulmonary edema. Oral prazosin is a specific alpha-blocker antidote that reverses cardiovascular collapse.

vis.alt: Infographic depicting the pathophysiology of scorpion venom autonomic storm, peripheral vasoconstriction, and reversal with prazosin.
vis.caption: Pathophysiology of red scorpion venom autonomic storm and therapeutic vasodilatation with prazosin. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Neurotoxic elapid and vasculotoxic viperid snake envenomations demand rapid syndromic identification and prompt polyvalent antivenom infusion. In **pediatric snakebite envenomation**, krait and cobra bites cause descending neuroparalysis with bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and respiratory arrest, while viper bites cause coagulopathy and hemotoxic bleeding, detected by the bedside twenty-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT), managed with Indian polyvalent antivenom.
steps.say: Neurotoxic krait and cobra bites cause ptosis and respiratory failure, while viper bites cause coagulopathy. A non-clotting twenty-minute blood test indicates urgent antivenom infusion.

rows: Bilateral ptosis, bulbar palsy, respiratory arrest
Local swelling, bleb, uncoagulable blood, bleeding
ASV based on 20-minute whole blood clotting test
Place 2 mL venous blood in glass tube x 20 min
Definitive indicator for initiating ASV therapy
10 vials reconstituted in normal saline IV
Infuse over 1 hour; repeat if coagulopathy persists
Epinephrine on standby for anaphylactic reactions
